title: Error Summary Report
story: Your automated test suite runs 5 checks on a dataset. Some pass, some fail — but you don't want the suite to stop on the first error. You need ALL checks to run, collecting successes and failures separately, then printing a summary: '3 passed, 2 failed (reasons: missing data, invalid format).' This is how test runners and batch processors work in production.
why: Collecting results from multiple fallible operations without short-circuiting teaches the accumulator pattern — essential for batch processing, test suites, and validation reports.
analogy: Running all checks without short-circuiting is like a car's annual inspection. The mechanic doesn't stop after finding a bald tire — they check the brakes, lights, emissions, and windshield too. At the end, you get a report: '3 items passed, 2 failed (tires: worn tread; lights: left blinker out).' You fix everything at once instead of making 5 separate trips to the shop.
try_it: Add 3 more checks: check that value is <= 100, check that value is at least 2 characters long, check that it doesn't contain '!'. Then run the full suite on 5 different values: "42", "-5", "0", "abc", "". Print a full report for each. Use an array of check functions if XIOM supports it. What percentage of checks passed? Add a 'pass rate' to the summary.
tips: Use `match`, NOT `?`, when you want all operations to run — `?` short-circuits and skips the rest
A tuple return `(Int, Int, Str)` is perfect for returning a summary — successes, failures, and error messages
Name each check descriptively — when the error report says 'check_positive failed', the user should understand what was checked
common_mistakes: Using `?` accidentally — `let r = check_a(val)?;` would stop processing on the first error
Forgetting to initialize the accumulator variables before the loop of checks
Concatenating error strings with `+` in XIOM can be finicky — make sure both sides are Str
